extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, university mathematics instructors, and assessment designers for academic development programmes
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, administering, and analysing a diagnostic mathematics test (pre/post) to measure students' mathematical (content-based) maturity and confidence within an academic development/extended programme. Includes item/topic classification, confidence reporting, and statistical analysis of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic maturity (two components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic maturity is subdivided into two components, namely, non-subject based maturity, and subject based maturity (mathematical maturity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's working framework measures both content based academic maturity (mathematical maturity) and non-content based academic maturity (social/behavioural). This decomposition motivates separate instruments/analyses for each component and comparison pre/post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical maturity (content-based = competence + confidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of this study, mathematical maturity (content based maturity) is defined as consisting of two components: mathematical competence (content knowledge) and mathematical confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement therefore requires both objective performance data (test scores) and self-reported confidence on each item; growth in maturity is assessed by change in both dimensions between pre- and post-tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-content based maturity (organisational/social/personal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioural (non-cognitive) traits are classified into organisational, social and personal maturity as part of the non-content based maturity framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this paper focuses on content-based maturity, non-content maturity is a parallel domain measured elsewhere (Yani et al., 2019) and should be considered when interpreting overall academic maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical competency taxonomy (Bothma/Niss dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bothma (2014) and Niss (2003) identify competency strands/dimensions used as measures of mathematical competence: knowing mathematics; communicating mathematics; doing and reasoning mathematics; representing mathematics; modelling and solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each dimension has a specific focus: 'knowing' = recognising and comprehending when to apply concepts and notation; 'doing and reasoning' = performing procedures and using tools; 'communicating' = correct use of symbols/language and precise written solutions; 'representing' = interpreting and converting representations; 'modelling and solving' = transforming real life issues into mathematical form and solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test content topic classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Test items are classified into six mathematical topics: algebraic expressions, algebraic equations, inequalities, functions and graphs, trigonometry, and logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topic classification is determined by the dominant method needed to solve the item; items that could fit multiple topics are assigned to the topic judged most dominant by a team of experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of items to taxonomy dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Items are grouped into the mathematical competency/taxonomy dimensions (e.g., doing and reasoning, representing, knowing, modelling/solving) according to how the item is solved and the theoretical dimension definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study items were mapped (by experts) to four dimensions for measurement: doing and reasoning mathematics (9 items), representing mathematics (2 items), knowing mathematics (4 items), and modelling and solving mathematical problems (1 item). Items potentially belong to multiple dimensions but experts choose the dominant classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument design: diagnostic test structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured diagnostic mathematics test of 16 content questions was administered twice (pre- and post-) with each content question immediately followed by a self-evaluation confidence question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pre- and post-tests were identical. Each content question carried one mark (total 16). Confidence responses used a four-point scale (1 not confident to 4 confident). Data from students who did not complete both tests or had incomplete identifying information were excluded from paired analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence index (CI) measurement and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Students indicated confidence for each item on a four-point scale from 1 (not confident) to 4 (confident); average CI per item and per student were calculated. An average confidence of 2.5 and above is regarded as high confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CI is used alongside correctness to reveal misconceptions vs lack of knowledge. Note the study references Hasan et al.'s six-point CI but implements a four-point CI; threshold 2.5 separates 'high' vs 'low' confidence in quadrant analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision matrix for distinguishing misconceptions vs lack of knowledge (Hasan et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Hasan et al.'s decision matrix: low CI with correct/incorrect answer indicates lack of knowledge (guessing or low certainty); high CI with correct answer indicates presence of knowledge; high CI with incorrect answer indicates presence of misconception (student strongly believes incorrect procedure is correct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The matrix combines correctness and CI per item to classify student responses; use this to target instruction (remediate misconceptions vs build knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrant analysis (CI vs Performance Score) with explicit quadrant labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot item averages of CI (y-axis) against performance score (PS, x-axis) and divide by thresholds: PS ≥ 50% (high mark) and CI ≥ 2.5 (high confidence) to create four quadrants: Quadrant 1 adequate knowledge (high CI, high PS); Quadrant 2 misconception (high CI, low PS); Quadrant 3 lack of knowledge (low CI, low PS); Quadrant 4 guessing (low CI, high PS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare pre-test quadrant positions to post-test to identify item-level shifts (e.g., items moving out of misconception quadrant). Use 50% as practical pass/high mark (context-specific).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre/post statistical comparison: paired-samples t-test
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare pre-test and post-test scores (and CI values) using paired-samples t-tests to determine whether change is statistically significant (report means, standard deviations, t, p, and 95% confidence intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct t-tests at item-level, topic-level, taxonomy-dimension-level, and student-level as appropriate. Report effect sizes alongside p-values to indicate practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation analysis between confidence and performance (Pearson's r) with interpretation bands
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the correlation between the confidence index and performance score using Pearson's correlation coefficient with a 95% confidence interval. Interpret r using bands: r ≤ 0.1 (non-linear / negligible), 0.11–0.29 (weak), 0.31–0.49 (moderate), 0.51–0.69 (strong), r ≥ 0.71 (very strong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correlation per item and aggregated levels to understand relationships between confidence and actual performance; use critical value r ≤ 0.1 for sample size considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size reporting (Cohen's d) and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate Cohen's d for pre/post differences to indicate practical significance; conventional benchmarks: small d = 0.2, medium d = 0.5, large d = 0.8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report effect sizes alongside p-values; a large Cohen's d indicates meaningful practical change even if p-values are small due to large N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and validity procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability (credibility) was enhanced via data source triangulation (administering the test twice to a prior cohort before use). Face validity (representative content coverage) and construct validity (measuring intended theoretical constructs) were established by expert classification of items into topics and dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot tests on earlier cohorts and expert review/classification are required to support face/construct validity. Report inter-rater procedures if multiple experts classify items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item scoring and aggregation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Each content question is scored 1 mark; total test score is sum over 16 items. Confidence scores are averaged across items to give per-item and per-student CI averages; performance score (PS) per student is average (or percentage) over the 16 items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these aggregated averages for t-tests, correlations, and quadrant plotting. Missing or incomplete data (e.g., incomplete student numbers) should be excluded from paired comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert decision rule for overlapping item classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When items could be categorised into more than one topic or taxonomy dimension, a team of experts decided which category was most dominant in the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply explicit adjudication rules and document rationale when assigning an item to a single dominant category; acknowledge possible classification ambiguity in limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant inclusion/exclusion criteria for paired analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Only students who participated in both the pre-test and the post-test with complete identifying information were analysed for change (e.g., N=385 in the paired sample); incomplete records were not considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Ns for pre-only, post-only, and paired samples; consider and report attrition effects and potential bias from dropouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual thresholds (pass/high mark and high confidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contextual thresholds appropriate to the institution: in this study 50% is the general pass/high mark for university courses in South Africa; an average confidence of 2.5 (on 1–4 scale) is regarded as high confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds are context-dependent and should be justified; quadrant labels and interpretations rely on these cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and interpretation caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term (one-semester) measurement, potential attrition of students (dropouts leaving course or changing fields), and inability to compare to higher levels of mathematics are limitations noted by the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the instrument, state temporal limits, account for dropout/mobility, and avoid overgeneralising short-term gains to long-term mathematical maturity without further longitudinal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument item examples and MCQ/CI pairing format
rubrics_metrics.description: The appendix provides the 16-item multiple-choice diagnostic test where each odd-numbered content question is followed by an even-numbered confidence question (answer choices a–f for content, and a–d for confidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the paired content/CI format if aiming to replicate the same analyses (decision matrix, quadrant analysis, item-level CI vs PS plots). Ensure item wording and choice plausibility support discrimination of misconceptions vs lack of knowledge.
